summary:
Almog Baku introduces the LLM Triangle Principles, a framework for building production-grade LLM applications. He emphasizes that while PoCs are easy, production is extremely hard due to edge cases. LLM-native applications are 10% sophisticated models and 90% hard experimentation and data-driven engineering. He compares LLMs to a new computational resource that shouldn't be programmed solely with traditional languages.

The framework has four pillars: Model, Engineering Techniques, Data, and SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) as the guiding principle. SOPs, borrowed from manufacturing, provide step-by-step instructions for consistent quality. LLMs are treated like brilliant but inexperienced interns requiring explicit prompting. Creating SOPs involves interviewing experts, reducing cognitive load by breaking tasks into steps, identifying hidden implicit cognition jumps, and describing the process as a graph.

Engineering techniques span prompt-level methods (chain of thought, few shots, role assumption) and software-level methods (chains, tools, fine-tuning), with hybrids like ReAct. LLM-native architecture splits SOPs into multiple agents—LLM plus prompt template components. Baku contrasts autonomous agents (creative but hard to debug, unsustainable quality) with crafted flows (predictable but expensive), recommending scoping autonomous agents with clear borders and using deterministic code wherever possible.

For model selection, Baku recommends starting with large models, collecting data, understanding the problem, then optimizing incrementally—potentially fine-tuning or switching models after months. Key considerations include task complexity, infrastructure, latency, cost, budget, and available data. He cautions against fine-tuning from day zero.

On data, he emphasizes that models are stateless—they receive a single text prompt, not separate context or system prompts. Prompt templates with variables help maintain sustainable code. He dismisses vendor claims about solving the needle-in-a-haystack problem, noting reality involves many needles in huge haystacks, requiring finding the right context balance. Few-shot examples embody show don't tell—teaching concepts difficult to describe in words. Dynamic example selection uses similarity mechanisms like vector search or logic-based selection to choose the best examples per use case. Baku concludes that data is king and the LLM Triangle—Model, Engineering Techniques, and Contextual Data, all guided by SOP—yields higher quality.

sections.title: Introduction and the Challenge of Production LLM Applications
sections.summary: Almog introduces himself and the talk topic. He notes that most LLM use cases today are small workflow enhancements, and while the future will be transformative, we need to shift our thinking about LLMs as a new computational resource.

sections.title: PoC vs Production and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Baku explains that building PoCs is easy but production applications are hard, with edge cases breaking during demos. He shares his background as a serial entrepreneur, founder of the AI Israel Community with 5,000 members, and his experience building dozens of LLM applications.

sections.title: The LLM Triangle Framework and SOPs
sections.summary: Introduces the four-pillar framework: Model, Engineering Techniques, Data, and SOP. Explains SOPs are borrowed from manufacturing—step-by-step instructions enabling consistent quality. LLMs should be treated like smart but inexperienced interns needing explicit prompting.

sections.title: Creating SOPs: Landing Page Builder Example
sections.summary: Walks through creating an SOP by interviewing or assuming the expert role, reducing cognitive load, identifying hidden implicit cognition jumps, compiling a list of steps, and describing the process as a graph to capture loops and recursions.

sections.title: Engineering Techniques and LLM-Native Architecture
sections.summary: Covers two categories of engineering techniques: prompt-level (chain of thought, few shots, role assumption) and software-level (chains, tools, fine-tuning), with hybrids like ReAct. Introduces LLM-native architecture as splitting the SOP into multiple agents, demonstrated with a Wikipedia writer example mixing LLM calls and deterministic code.

sections.title: Agents, Autonomous Agents, and Crafted Flows
sections.summary: Defines an agent as LLM plus prompt template. Contrasts autonomous agents (given tools and decision rights—elegant, creative, fast but hard to debug, unsustainable quality) with crafted flows (predictable, debuggable, sustainable but expensive). Recommends scoping autonomous agents with clear borders.

sections.title: Model Selection Strategy
sections.summary: Covers model selection considerations: task complexity, infrastructure for open-source vs proprietary models, latency, cost, budget constraints, and available data. Presents a chart showing large models are expensive but broadly capable, smaller models suit simpler tasks or ample-data scenarios, and smaller models underperform on complex tasks. Recommends starting with large models, collecting data, then optimizing incrementally rather than fine-tuning from day zero.

sections.title: Contextual Data and Prompt Templates
sections.summary: Emphasizes data as the most important part of the talk. Explains models are stateless—receiving a single text prompt, not separate system or user prompts—and that prompt templates with variables help maintain sustainable code. Discusses the needle-in-a-haystack problem, dismissing vendor claims since reality involves many needles in a huge haystack. Stresses finding the right balance of context—not too much, not too little.

sections.title: Few Shots and Dynamic Example Selection
sections.summary: Demonstrates few-shot learning with a product classification example showing how examples shift the model's output language to match desired vibes. Introduces show don't tell as a key principle. Covers dynamic example selection where companies select a handful of best examples per use case using similarity mechanisms like vector search or logic-based selection by keyword or category.

sections.title: Conclusion: The LLM Triangle Recap
sections.summary: Recaps the LLM Triangle: three key principles—Model, Engineering Techniques, and Contextual Data—all guided by SOP. Baku states data is king without data we don't have a kingdom, and encourages attendees to reach out on LinkedIn and read the full white paper.
